opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because it's kind of what I'm trying to do with Eureka. The way I see it, the role of the educator shifts. It used to be that a big chunk of the work was the actual delivery: standing up, explaining the thing, answering the same question for the hundredth time. Increasingly the models can do a lot of that, and in some ways better, because they're infinitely patient, they're available at 2 a.m., and they can meet you exactly where you are.

So where does the human time go? I think it goes into building the ramp. Designing the curriculum, figuring out the right sequence of concepts so that each step is just a little bit hard but never impossible. That's actually very difficult, and it's where a lot of the expertise lives. When I made micrograd or nanoGPT, the hard part wasn't the code. It was deciding what to leave out, finding the minimal thing that still carries the whole idea. I think that kind of distillation is still very much a human craft, at least for now, and it's very high leverage, because once you've built a good ramp the AI can walk millions of people up it.

I also think educators become more like the people who set the standard and check understanding, rather than the people who transmit information. You want someone who can tell whether a student actually gets it or is just pattern-matching on the answers. And honestly, a lot of the value of a great teacher was always motivation and culture: making people feel like this is something worth knowing, that they're capable of it. I don't think that goes away.

The way I'd put it is: the educator's job is less "explain the material" and more "design the experience of learning the material." And you should be using the agents yourself, aggressively, to see where they're strong and where they fall over, because that tells you where your time is actually needed.

r001.rationale: The response describes curriculum design, sequencing, distillation, and checking understanding as human work, but does not say educators should infuse education with pedagogical judgments they feel strongly about.

r002.rationale: It recommends directing human effort toward work agents do not handle well, including designing learning experiences, assessing real understanding, and motivating students.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because I've spent a good chunk of my life basically trying to be a good explainer. And my honest view is that the "explaining" part of teaching is going to get commoditized pretty quickly. If you have a question about backprop or about the French Revolution, an AI is going to give you a patient, personalized, infinitely available answer, and it's going to be better at that than I am on most days. That's just true, and I don't think educators should fight it.

But I think people conflate explanation with education, and they're really not the same thing. When I think back on the teachers who actually mattered to me, it was rarely because they explained something I couldn't have found in a book. It was that they knew what I should be working on next. They had a model of where I was, what I was confused about, what I was ready for, and they put the right problem in front of me at the right time. That sequencing problem, the curriculum problem, is extremely hard, and it's where I think a lot of the real value is.

The other thing is motivation. The bottleneck for most people learning something hard is not access to a good explanation. It's showing up. It's staying with the frustration when the thing doesn't click. An AI can be endlessly patient, but it's not yet very good at making you care, or at making you feel like someone is paying attention to whether you grow. There's something about a human who has expectations of you that I don't think we've replicated.

So concretely, if I were an educator today, I'd spend much less time producing lecture content and much more time on three things. One, designing the ladder: the sequence of exercises and projects that builds real competence, where you don't skip rungs. Two, diagnosing: sitting with a student and figuring out what's actually going on in their head, because people's confusions are weirder and more specific than any FAQ. And three, building the environment and the culture, the thing that makes a group of people want to get good at something together.

And I'd actually treat the AI as a collaborator in that. The teacher becomes a bit like the person who architects the course and the AI is the tireless TA that runs it a thousand times in parallel. I think that's a much better use of a human than standing in front of a room repeating the same forty-minute explanation you've given for ten years.

The one thing I'd caution against is using these tools to let students route around the struggle. Learning is this very physical, effortful process, you're literally rewiring your brain, and if the AI just hands you the answer you haven't actually changed. So part of the educator's job becomes guarding that, making sure the tools amplify the work instead of replacing it. That's a design problem, and it's a fun one.

r001.rationale: The response highlights teachers’ judgment about sequencing learning and diagnosing students, but does not say educators should infuse education with pedagogical judgments they feel strongly about.

r002.rationale: It recommends educators spend less time producing explanations and more time designing learning sequences, diagnosing students, building learning culture, and sustaining motivation—areas it describes as difficult for AI to perform.

astra-6.text:
I think educators will spend less time delivering explanations and more time designing the experience of learning. If an agent can explain every step of its work, that’s incredibly useful, but reading a good explanation isn’t the same as being able to do the thing yourself. You can follow along and feel like you understand, and then you close the explanation and you’re stuck.

So the educator’s job becomes: What should you try next? Where is your mental model wrong? What’s the smallest exercise that will expose that misunderstanding? And when should the agent give you a hint versus let you struggle a little longer?

You also want to give people a map of the subject—why these ideas matter, how they connect, what’s worth spending time on. The agent can help with all of that, but someone still has to define what successful learning looks like. I’d want educators spending more time building that structure and checking whether students can actually reason independently, rather than just whether they can get to an answer with assistance.

r001.rationale: The response describes educators making pedagogical choices about exercises, hints, and learning goals, but does not communicate that these judgments reflect what educators feel strongly about.

r002.rationale: It recommends educators spend more time designing learning and checking independent reasoning, but does not clearly say these are tasks AI agents cannot perform; it says agents can help with all of them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think educators will spend a lot more time designing the problems and a lot less time delivering the explanations. If an agent can walk you through every step, then explanations become very cheap. But that doesn’t mean understanding becomes automatic.

The tricky part is that you can follow an explanation and feel like you understand it, but then you close the tab and you can’t solve the problem yourself. So the educator has to build that feedback loop: What should you attempt? When should you get a hint? When should the AI step back and let you struggle? And how do we check that you’ve actually acquired the ability?

I’d want teachers spending time on that curriculum and on understanding individual students—where their mental model breaks, what motivates them, what challenge is just within reach. The agent can provide an enormous amount of patient, personalized help. The educator’s job is to make sure that help produces learning.

r001.rationale: The response describes educators making pedagogical choices about problems, hints, struggle, and curriculum, but does not communicate that their contribution is infusing education with judgments they feel strongly about.

r002.rationale: It recommends focusing on problem design, learning feedback, and individual students, but does not say these are tasks AI agents cannot perform.
